body: Enabling safe access to the Arctic is expected to lead to more cost effective and environmentally friendly exploitation of resources in the Arctic, including shipping routes from Northern Europe to East Asia (Northeast Passage) and North America (Northwest Passage). Indeed, shipping transportation in the Arctic passage is now a real alternative to the southern routes through the Suez Canal. In early 2018, a shipping vessel Eduard Toll, made a winter crossing of the Arctic without an icebreaker for the first time as global warming causes the region’s ice sheets to melt. Measurements and detection of icebergs, sea ice thickness, and snow on ice are today done from satellite, aircraft and in-situ on the ice

[50]. Each method has its limitations and advantages. From satellite, optical, radar, and passive microwave sensors are used. Snow cover is, however, only measured through passive microwave and is only accurate on regional scales, and the resolution is typically on the scale of several kilometers. Research-mode satellites provide resolution down to one meter, and when combined with multiple polarizations this allows for characterization of ridges, both for first- and multi-year ice. Optical satellites like Sentinel-2 have resolution down to 10 meters for ice concentration but have limitations due to clouds and light conditions on the visual bands. Airborne measurements of sea-ice thickness are currently conducted by helicopter or fixed-wing aircraft. These platforms are equipped with an electromagnetic-induction (EM) sensor that has to be carried very close to the ice (10-30 meters) and a laser altimeter and measure the combined ice and snow thickness. Towing the EM bird at these altitudes are high-risk operations and are therefore limited. For accurate positioning of aircraft, the current state-of-the-art is to use high precision GPS combined with laser altimeter. Using laser scanners or altimeters alone for measuring free-board to estimate ice thickness was done by Crocker et al [51], but introduces large errors due to the different densities between snow and ice. The Norwegian Research Center (NORCE) [52] has developed an ultra-wide band (UWB) radar that can estimate the thickness of the snow layer, hence making this approach feasible.
